Lesson No. 57: Explanation of the Verses

Verses 12 to 19

Verses 12 and 13

Here the address is one of clarification and decision. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is instructed to address those polytheists who well know that Allah alone is the Creator, yet who, despite knowing this, set up as equals to the Creator those who are themselves created beings. And further, in their own assumption, they also make these partners involved in the affairs of their own lives. The question is put to them: if you accept that Allah is the Creator, then tell us, after creation, who is the Owner? That is, who is the Creator of this entire universe, of the heavens and the earth? Who is the Owner of whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Then the answer is given by the same question itself, because they did not deny it: "Say: To Allah." Had the Arabs been asked, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?", they would have answered, "To Allah." It thus becomes clear that even while being in the darkness of jahiliyyah and suffering from intellectual and theoretical misguidance, they were nevertheless far better than the jahiliyyah of the modern age. The jahiliyyah of the modern age may be called a jahiliyyah of knowledge, because it denies even this simple reality, that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah. It has blinded its own nature, and it does not see even this self-evident truth.

The followers of Arab jahiliyyah, although they perceived this self-evident truth, and held the belief that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, nevertheless did not draw the logical consequences of this acknowledgment and affirmation. Thus they did not regard Allah as the absolute ruler and supreme authority even over His own possessions. They did not confine all their dealings and all their movements and rests in the world within the bounds of the permission of Allah. This is why they were declared mushrikun, and were called the people of jahiliyyah. As for those who exclude all their affairs from the sphere of Allah's sovereignty and make themselves the rulers of their own lives, then it can now be asked of them: what should we call them, and what judgment should we pass on their lives? Clearly, no title other than mushrikun can be given to such people, nor can their lives be described as anything other than a life of shirk. For, according to the very judgment of Allah, their life is one of transgression, oppression and disbelief, however much they may claim Islam (whatever religion their birth certificates may state, since those are merely filled in at the time of birth).

Now let us look closely at the verse. After affirming that the Owner of the heavens and the earth is He, it adds: "(Kataba ala nafsihi al-rahmah)", "He has made mercy binding upon Himself." Allah alone is the Creator and Owner, and there is no partner with Him who could contest. Yet, by His bounty and mercy, He has made it binding upon Himself that He is Raouf and Raheem. By His will, His purpose and His good pleasure, He has adopted this attitude; no one else has imposed this attitude upon Allah, nor has anyone demanded it of Him. By His absolute will and by the generous majesty of His lordship, He has taken on this merciful conduct. And this principle Allah has established as a settled rule for Himself in His decisions, His character and His dealings, both in this world and in the Hereafter. This principle also operates within the foundations of the Islamic conception of life and Islamic beliefs. The original principle is that Allah shows mercy to His servants; even if Allah afflicts a servant with trials and calamities, in reality compassion is intended in it. He places His servants in difficulties so that among them there may always be ready an element capable of bearing the burden of the trust of Allah, and this great trust is entrusted to a group when it becomes ready for bearing this burden in terms of its sincerity, its selflessness, its understanding and perception, and its preparation and experience. Wicked forces are removed and cast out from the ranks of the pure and the clean, and it becomes clearly known who is truly obedient to the Messenger and who is a runaway. Whoever perishes, perishes with understanding, and whoever survives, survives upon principles. All these matters lie within the sphere of Allah's mercy.

The life of man is filled with the occasions of Allah's mercy. Every moment and every instant displays a new aspect of His compassion and mercy. We have mentioned the period of trial and hardship only because at times the thinking and vision of people is deceived in it.

It is not our purpose here to enumerate the matters and manifestations of Allah's mercy; some manifestations you will see in the coming pages. Our aim here is only to reflect a little on this verse, and to see what is really meant by "(Kataba ala nafsihi al-rahmah)". The same truth is stated elsewhere in this surah in these words: "(Kataba rabbukum ala nafsihi al-rahmah)" ("Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy"). What is striking in this verse is precisely that bounty and generosity to which we have pointed. That is, a Supreme Being who is Creator, Owner and possessor of irresistible power displays bounty and mercy instead of using His irresistible power, and moreover in such a way that He has written this act upon Himself, made it obligatory upon Himself. Of His own accord He has signed this covenant. By His absolute will and purpose alone He is bestowing grace upon us. This is a great truth which, when a person keeps it before him, reflects upon it, and observes its wondrous manner, must necessarily have a good effect upon his personality, his thought and his taste of perception.

Further, it is also striking that Allah Himself informs His servants of this attribute of His mercy, that I have written this principle upon Myself, have made it obligatory upon Myself, that I shall certainly show bounty and mercy. Now, who are the servants concerning whom this decision has been made in the higher realm, and whose command has reached them in written form, that a decision has been made concerning them, and that it is being conveyed to them through the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Who are these people? They are not some special people; rather they are ordinary people, and this bounty and mercy of Allah is for all people.

By reflecting in this manner upon this truth, strange and wondrous thoughts arise in the heart. A person is astonished. In his heart there arises such intimacy and such spiritual delight that it cannot be expressed in words. These truths of the heart and vision leave impressions which a person can taste and can feel, but their expression in human speech is not possible, nor can they be fully described.

From this truth it becomes evident that in the Islamic conception of life the attribute of mercy is the foundational aspect of the divine reality. Upon it the relationship of servitude between the servant and the Divine is established, and this conception is most beautiful and delightful, filled with love and affection. In light of this foundational conception, every fair-minded person will be greatly surprised at the mentality of those ill-natured people and at their slanders, that they make statements against the Islamic conception of the Divine which are contrary to reality. They make these accusations because Islam does not believe in the "sonship" doctrine. Islam does not accept that any of Allah's servants can be His son, whereas the Church, by deviating from the Gospel, fabricated this belief. The Islamic conception of life regarding the generous majesty of Allah is very lofty and exalted, and this "Kaniseh" is far above childish imaginings. The relationship of compassion and love between Allah and the servant is beyond human words. Along with the majesty of Allah it can be felt, but it cannot be described.

The overflowing of Allah's mercy reaches all His servants. This mercy embraces everyone in its shelter. It is through this mercy that the human self remains alive; the bond between his body and soul is firmly established. In the human existence and in the existence of this entire universe, the mercy of Allah and His generous majesty continually flow. As far as human life and the human body are concerned, we cannot count the occasions of Allah's mercy within them. Nevertheless, it is necessary to mention some of its outstanding aspects and manifestations.

First of all, the mercy of Allah is seen in the very self of man. Allah creates man in such a way that man himself has no knowledge of it. Human beings themselves do not know how this existence was granted to them. Then within him have been placed such distinctive qualities that through them man has been given superiority over all created beings.

Then His generous majesty is seen in the powers which man has, until today, been able to subdue. This universe and its powers, and this is Allah's provision in its broader meaning, may be understood thus: the universe, in whose vast fields man at all times displays his prowess.

Then the manifestation of this generous majesty is also seen in the fact that Allah bestowed knowledge upon man. First He granted him the capacity to acquire knowledge, and He created harmony between his faculties and the powers of this universe. This knowledge, by means of which some ill-natured and bad-tempered human beings begin to lay hands even upon the Divine Being, while it is He who conferred this knowledge upon those ill-natured people, and this knowledge is one of the provisions from Allah.

Then this generous majesty is also manifested in that Allah, by appointing man as His vicegerent in this world, arranged for his care and upbringing by sending messengers continuously for his guidance. Whenever man strayed, Allah guided him and, with great love and patience, set him again upon the straight path. Although at times man did not even give ear to the voices of those warning and admonishing messengers, it was not difficult for Allah to destroy him; yet the attribute of Allah's mercy always granted him respite, and always the forbearance of Allah covered man.

Then the manifestation of this generous majesty is also seen in the fact that when a servant commits a sin out of ignorance and then repents, Allah forgives him, and this is because Allah has made it binding upon Himself to show mercy.

It is also an aspect of His generous majesty that for an evil He records only one evil and punishes only for that one evil, but for a good deed He bestows the reward of ten good deeds, and beyond that He may increase for whomever He wills in his record of deeds. Moreover, Allah also keeps erasing the reward of good deeds, and all this is His bounty. Furthermore, no one can attain Paradise merely by the strength of his own deeds unless His grace is included in his favour. Even the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself said about himself that he too would enter Paradise by the grace of Allah. If the grace and bounty of Allah were not included, man would be most helpless.

In sum, rather than giving detailed accounts of the occasions and manifestations of Allah's mercy, generosity and bounty, it is better for us to declare our own shortcoming of understanding, and to say that it is difficult for us to fully comprehend His generous majesty, and that this is the appropriate attitude for us. For if we do not do so, and do not declare that we have failed, we cannot succeed in this field. The moment in which the doors of Allah's mercy open upon a servant, he attains access to Allah. He becomes filled with knowledge of his Lord; he attains peace and tranquillity. He takes refuge in the shelter of His compassion, and seeks refuge at His threshold. Even a single brief moment contains such vastness that it is not possible for any human being to describe or explain it; indeed, it is impossible for a person to fully express the generous majesty of Allah.

Consider carefully how the Noble Messenger (ﷺ), through his concise and comprehensive words and beautiful parables, sought to bring the generous majesty of Allah close to our understanding and our intellect. Al-Shaykhan, with their chains of narration, related from Abu Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When Allah had decreed the creations (Imam Muslim said: when Allah had created the creatures), He wrote in a Book which is with Him upon the Throne: "My mercy has preceded My wrath." Imam al-Bukhari gave in another narration the words: "My mercy has overcome My anger."

Al-Shaykhan, through their chain, related from Abu Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah divided mercy into one hundred parts, of which He has retained ninety-nine with Himself, and has sent down upon the earth only one part. By using this one part, creatures show mercy to one another, so much so that an animal lifts its hooves lest it should step upon its young."

Imam Muslim, through his chain, related from Salman al-Farisi (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has one hundred mercies. By using one of these mercies, the creatures of Allah deal with one another with compassion, and Allah has reserved ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection."

In another narration from him: "On the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, He created one hundred mercies. Each mercy of Allah is greater than the heavens and the earth. Of these, Allah gave only one mercy for use upon the earth. By this mercy a mother shows compassion to her child, and wild animals and birds show mercy to one another. When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will complete this mercy with the remaining ninety-nine parts."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the extent of mercy through images, only to bring it closer to human understanding. When a person observes among living creatures how mothers treat their children with such compassion, and how people show kindness to their children, and likewise to the elderly, the weak, the sick, relatives, friends and offspring, and also how birds and wild animals treat one another, he is overcome with amazement. Some of these scenes are so striking that they overwhelm a person, and he then reflects that this is only one part out of a hundred parts of Allah's generous mercy, and he becomes even more astonished. This method of explanation brings the matter close to people's minds. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ constantly made his Companions aware of this great mercy.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: Some female prisoners of war were brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among them was a woman who was running about, and milk was flowing from her breasts. Whenever she found a child among the captive women's camp, she would seize it, press it to her stomach and nurse it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire?" We said: "By Allah, if she has the power not to do so (i.e., is not compelled), she would never do it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Know that Allah has more love for His servants than this woman has for her child." (Bukhari, Muslim)

How could it not be so? The compassion and tenderness this woman has for her child is a blessing of that mercy which Allah has bestowed upon the inhabitants of the earth from His vast mercy.

The teaching that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave his Companions of this kind resulted in his taking one step further and commanding his Companions to adopt the character of Allah in this matter. They were to treat one another with mercy and affection, show mercy to all living creatures of this world, and let a taste for love and compassion arise in their hearts, so that they would practise this taste in all their affairs, just as Allah deals with His creatures with mercy. This aspect of the teachings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is extremely vibrant and radiant. Let us observe some examples.

Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Those who show mercy will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Show mercy to those on the earth, and He who is in the heavens will show mercy to you." (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi)

Narrated from Ibn Jarir (may Allah be pleased with him), who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah does not show mercy to one who does not show mercy to people." (Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi)

Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi have stated, in a narration from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Mercy is taken away only from one who is hard-hearted."

Similarly, Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kissed Hasan ibn Ali, and at that time Aqra ibn Habis was sitting beside him. Aqra said: "I have ten children, and I have never kissed any one of them." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at him and said: "Whoever does not show compassion, compassion will not be shown to him." (Muslim, Bukhari)

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not merely teach his Companions to treat only human beings kindly, because he knew that Allah's mercy is very vast and that Muslims had been commanded to develop the character of Allah within themselves. A person cannot become a complete human being until he treats all creation with mercy. In this regard, his teachings were extremely effective, as we have already mentioned.

Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It happened that a man, during a journey, was walking along a path when he was overcome by severe thirst. He found a well, descended into it, drank water and came out. Then he saw a dog panting from thirst and eating earth because of the intensity of its thirst. The man said: 'This dog has been reduced to the same state by thirst as I had been.' So he went down into the well again, filled his shoe with water, held it in his mouth until he came out, and gave the dog water to drink. Allah accepted this from him, rewarded him and forgave him." The Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there a reward for us in (showing kindness to) animals?" He ﷺ said: "There is a reward in (showing mercy to) every living creature with a moist liver." (Bukhari, Muslim, Muwatta)

In another narration, it is related that a sinful woman once saw a dog circling a well in intense heat, its tongue hanging out from thirst. She made a bucket of her shoe and a rope of her headscarf, drew water for it and gave it to drink, and Allah forgave her.

Abdul Rahman ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from his father, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey. We saw a bird (a humrah) with two young ones with it, and we seized the young ones. The bird came and was fluttering over the ground (that is, it was drawing close to the earth with its wings loosened and spread). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and said: "Who has caused distress to her on account of her young? Return her young to her." He ﷺ also saw that we had burned an anthill, so he asked: "Who burned this?" We said: "We burned it." He ﷺ said: "No one should punish with fire except the Lord of the fire." (Abu Dawud)

Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A prophet was bitten by an ant. He ordered that its colony be burned. Allah revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, will you destroy an entire community which glorifies Allah?'" (Muslim, Bukhari)

In this way, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ trained his Companions, in accordance with this teaching of the Noble Qur'an, so that they would taste the mercy of Allah in such a way that they would extend it to people. Is it not a fact that the mercy and compassion which creatures show to one another is one of the countless and priceless mercies of Allah?

Now I wish to state that when the reality of mercy becomes settled in a Muslim's conception of life, it has profound effects on his feelings, his life and his character, and these can never be erased in any form. Here, in keeping with the concise style of Fi Zilal al-Quran, we shall also point out briefly the effects that the above teaching has on the life of a Muslim.

As a result of awareness of this reality, the heart of the believer is enriched with the wealth of tranquillity, and he becomes fully content with his Lord. This is especially so in circumstances when he is passing through difficulties and severe moments, because in trials and hardships a person's heart and sight may be deceived. Thus the believer, beset by difficulties, always hopes for the mercy of Allah and believes that circumstances can change at any moment, and that after every situation a new situation may arise. Allah does not abandon His servants to difficulties, nor deprive them of His mercy, because whoever seeks Allah's mercy, Allah will not deprive him. It is people who deprive themselves of Allah's mercy by being ungrateful to Him, refusing to come under the shade of His mercy, and fleeing from it. Then, through firm contentment in hope of Allah's mercy, patience and steadfastness arise within a person, the light of hope shines, and he feels ease and rest, because he is in the court of mercy and love whose shade is dense, so long as he does not himself distance himself from it.

When a Muslim attains this awareness, a sense of modesty before the Creator arises in his feelings, because despite hope for forgiveness and the desire for the mercy of the Lord, no one should dare to disobey Allah. Indeed, through this hope one should feel shame at disobeying Allah, the Forgiving and Merciful. Those in whom the mercy and forgiveness of Allah give rise to a further urge to commit sin have, in truth, never tasted the sweetness of the reality of faith. Therefore, neither do I understand, nor do I accept, what some Sufis say: that they commit sins so that they may taste Allah's forbearance and clemency, or benefit from His forgiveness and mercy. This is not the thinking of people of sound nature; it is a negative reaction to the mercy of God.

After grasping this reality in this manner, very good effects arise in the mind of a Muslim. He knows that he must develop within himself the character of Allah. He also knows that the showers of Allah's mercies are falling upon him from every direction, despite his being full of shortcomings and sins occurring from him. In this way, he himself learns the ways of mercy and tenderness; he knows how to forgive, he overlooks sins and mistakes. This is clearly visible to us in the teachings that the Messenger ﷺ gave to his Companions, and this teaching he imparted through "takhalluq bi-akhlaq Allah" (adopting the character of Allah). One of the stations of Allah's mercy is that He has written upon Himself that He will gather all human beings on a day in the field of assembly. This verse also decides this:

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah. He has prescribed mercy upon Himself. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt."﴾ (6:12)

Included in this claim of Allah's written mercy is that He will gather them again on a day, and this is an unalterable reality. After this gathering, the favours of Allah will be manifest, and these favours will be for those who worship Him, because Allah created them precisely so that they would take the path of worshipping Allah throughout their whole lives. They were given the office of vicegerency on this earth solely for this purpose. They were not created without purpose, nor are they left aimless. There is a day coming on which all these people will be assembled. This is the final destination to which they will return, just as a caravan moves steadily toward its intended goal. There Allah will reward those who adopted the correct path toward Allah and bore hardships during this long journey of life. The good deeds they performed in the world will be recompensed there, so that their exertions and hardships are not lost, but rather they will be given their full reward on the Day of Judgment. Thus one of the manifestations of Allah's mercies will be displayed. The grace of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, whereby the recompense for an evil deed will be only its like, while the reward for a good deed will be ten times, and indeed, if Allah wills, multiplied many times over, will also be one of the manifestations of Allah's mercy and compassion.

The grace and generosity that Allah bestowed upon the Arabs through the religion of Islam, and the honourable station He gave them through this religion, is a great favour of Allah upon them. Before this, the Arabs denied the Resurrection. They held exactly the same ideas as the thinking of the modern civilised ignorance, that is, scientific ignorance. For this reason, the mention of the Resurrection was made in such emphatic words, and against this denial, such emphatic particles were brought.

﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt.﴾ (6:12)

On the Day of Resurrection, loss will befall only those who in this world remained deprived of faith. Those who believe will suffer no loss, whereas the disbelievers will suffer complete loss, because they have lost their very selves, so what will they earn? A person earns for his own soul and self. If his self and his tongue are gone, for whom will he earn, and for whom will he work?

﴿Those who have lost themselves, so they do not believe.﴾ (6:12)

"But those who have put themselves into the danger of ruin do not believe in it." They lost their very selves in loss; their self and personality went away, and since they no longer had any personality, who would believe? This is a very subtle and realistic expression of the condition of the disbelievers. Within this expression there is a deeply natural call: believe! One of the great blessings of faith is that it grants you a self and a personality. Those who lost their personality before faith, whose nature had been corrupted, whose capacities that accept truth had been destroyed or veiled, lost their identity and individuality by losing the capacity to accept truth. This is why they did not believe, because they no longer had their own self and personality. This is a very subtle and profound description of their lack of tranquillity and of their disbelief. Yet the proofs of faith were present, and there were indications by which a person accepts truth; this matter became decisive in their case. Thus, having washed their hands of their own personality, they suffered a barren loss.

Now the next verse tells us that the people and creatures of night and day, that is, of time, also belong to Him. Just as the earlier verses stated that whatever living being is in any place and any space is the possession of Allah, so ownership now encompasses both time and space. Allah's knowledge encompasses all creatures.

(وَلَهُ مَا سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ ۚ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ) "To Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." (6:13)

"Whatever dwells in the night and the day, all of it belongs to Allah, and He hears and knows everything." 

The most readily understood interpretation of (مَا سَكَنَ) is that it derives from sakana (to dwell, to take refuge), as Zamakhshari wrote in al-Kashshaf: that is, everything that takes refuge in night and day, meaning all creation. All of this creation is in Allah's ownership. The previous verse also established this: (قُل لِّمَن مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۗ قُل لِّلَّهِ) "Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah." (6:12). That verse expressed the scope of all creation in terms of place, whereas this verse, (وَلَهُ مَا سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ) (6:13), expresses it in terms of time. This is a well-known mode of expression in the Holy Qur'an. Much has been written in the commentary of these verses, but in my view the best explanation is that one verse restricts ownership by time and the other by place.

After this comes the remark that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, from which it is understood that, in respect of knowledge too, Allah encompasses all creatures. In response to this verse, whatever the polytheists say is within Allah's knowledge. That is, even while acknowledging that Allah alone is the Owner, they nevertheless set aside certain livestock, their young, and certain fruits for their partners. This discussion recurs at the end of this surah. Here Allah demands that people acknowledge His rightful ownership of all creation, so that later it may be explained to them by whose authority they assign some of Allah's creatures to the account of their partners. Along with this, the phrase also aims to establish that since He is the Owner, He is also the Guardian and the Ruler, and He is the Ruler because He is the Owner of everything within time and space, and within Allah's knowledge.

Now that it is established that He is the Creator and the Owner, severe rebuke and criticism is directed at those who seek help from anyone other than Allah, who worship anyone other than Allah, and who take others as guardians and rulers. Thus it is decided that this state of affairs is contrary to Islam; it is clear polytheism, and it cannot be combined with Islam. Here, to convey this meaning, attributes of Allah such as Fatir al-Samawat wal-Ard (Originator of the heavens and the earth), Razzaq and Mut'im (Provider and Feeder), Nafi' and Darr (the Benefiter and the Harmer), and Qahir and Qadir (the Subduer and the Powerful) are brought forth, while it is also stated that He inflicts a dreadful punishment. Thereupon the atmosphere is suddenly overshadowed by the majesty of Allah, the person is struck with fear, and this is said with great force:

Lesson No. 57: Explanation of the Verses

Verses 12 to 19

Verses 12 and 13

Here the address is one of clarification and decision. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is instructed to address those polytheists who well know that Allah alone is the Creator, yet who, despite knowing this, set up as equals to the Creator those who are themselves created beings. And further, in their own assumption, they also make these partners involved in the affairs of their own lives. The question is put to them: if you accept that Allah is the Creator, then tell us, after creation, who is the Owner? That is, who is the Creator of this entire universe, of the heavens and the earth? Who is the Owner of whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Then the answer is given by the same question itself, because they did not deny it: "Say: To Allah." Had the Arabs been asked, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?", they would have answered, "To Allah." It thus becomes clear that even while being in the darkness of jahiliyyah and suffering from intellectual and theoretical misguidance, they were nevertheless far better than the jahiliyyah of the modern age. The jahiliyyah of the modern age may be called a jahiliyyah of knowledge, because it denies even this simple reality, that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah. It has blinded its own nature, and it does not see even this self-evident truth.

The followers of Arab jahiliyyah, although they perceived this self-evident truth, and held the belief that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, nevertheless did not draw the logical consequences of this acknowledgment and affirmation. Thus they did not regard Allah as the absolute ruler and supreme authority even over His own possessions. They did not confine all their dealings and all their movements and rests in the world within the bounds of the permission of Allah. This is why they were declared mushrikun, and were called the people of jahiliyyah. As for those who exclude all their affairs from the sphere of Allah's sovereignty and make themselves the rulers of their own lives, then it can now be asked of them: what should we call them, and what judgment should we pass on their lives? Clearly, no title other than mushrikun can be given to such people, nor can their lives be described as anything other than a life of shirk. For, according to the very judgment of Allah, their life is one of transgression, oppression and disbelief, however much they may claim Islam (whatever religion their birth certificates may state, since those are merely filled in at the time of birth).

Now let us look closely at the verse. After affirming that the Owner of the heavens and the earth is He, it adds: "(Kataba ala nafsihi al-rahmah)", "He has made mercy binding upon Himself." Allah alone is the Creator and Owner, and there is no partner with Him who could contest. Yet, by His bounty and mercy, He has made it binding upon Himself that He is Raouf and Raheem. By His will, His purpose and His good pleasure, He has adopted this attitude; no one else has imposed this attitude upon Allah, nor has anyone demanded it of Him. By His absolute will and by the generous majesty of His lordship, He has taken on this merciful conduct. And this principle Allah has established as a settled rule for Himself in His decisions, His character and His dealings, both in this world and in the Hereafter. This principle also operates within the foundations of the Islamic conception of life and Islamic beliefs. The original principle is that Allah shows mercy to His servants; even if Allah afflicts a servant with trials and calamities, in reality compassion is intended in it. He places His servants in difficulties so that among them there may always be ready an element capable of bearing the burden of the trust of Allah, and this great trust is entrusted to a group when it becomes ready for bearing this burden in terms of its sincerity, its selflessness, its understanding and perception, and its preparation and experience. Wicked forces are removed and cast out from the ranks of the pure and the clean, and it becomes clearly known who is truly obedient to the Messenger and who is a runaway. Whoever perishes, perishes with understanding, and whoever survives, survives upon principles. All these matters lie within the sphere of Allah's mercy.

The life of man is filled with the occasions of Allah's mercy. Every moment and every instant displays a new aspect of His compassion and mercy. We have mentioned the period of trial and hardship only because at times the thinking and vision of people is deceived in it.

It is not our purpose here to enumerate the matters and manifestations of Allah's mercy; some manifestations you will see in the coming pages. Our aim here is only to reflect a little on this verse, and to see what is really meant by "(Kataba ala nafsihi al-rahmah)". The same truth is stated elsewhere in this surah in these words: "(Kataba rabbukum ala nafsihi al-rahmah)" ("Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy"). What is striking in this verse is precisely that bounty and generosity to which we have pointed. That is, a Supreme Being who is Creator, Owner and possessor of irresistible power displays bounty and mercy instead of using His irresistible power, and moreover in such a way that He has written this act upon Himself, made it obligatory upon Himself. Of His own accord He has signed this covenant. By His absolute will and purpose alone He is bestowing grace upon us. This is a great truth which, when a person keeps it before him, reflects upon it, and observes its wondrous manner, must necessarily have a good effect upon his personality, his thought and his taste of perception.

Further, it is also striking that Allah Himself informs His servants of this attribute of His mercy, that I have written this principle upon Myself, have made it obligatory upon Myself, that I shall certainly show bounty and mercy. Now, who are the servants concerning whom this decision has been made in the higher realm, and whose command has reached them in written form, that a decision has been made concerning them, and that it is being conveyed to them through the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Who are these people? They are not some special people; rather they are ordinary people, and this bounty and mercy of Allah is for all people.

By reflecting in this manner upon this truth, strange and wondrous thoughts arise in the heart. A person is astonished. In his heart there arises such intimacy and such spiritual delight that it cannot be expressed in words. These truths of the heart and vision leave impressions which a person can taste and can feel, but their expression in human speech is not possible, nor can they be fully described.

From this truth it becomes evident that in the Islamic conception of life the attribute of mercy is the foundational aspect of the divine reality. Upon it the relationship of servitude between the servant and the Divine is established, and this conception is most beautiful and delightful, filled with love and affection. In light of this foundational conception, every fair-minded person will be greatly surprised at the mentality of those ill-natured people and at their slanders, that they make statements against the Islamic conception of the Divine which are contrary to reality. They make these accusations because Islam does not believe in the "sonship" doctrine. Islam does not accept that any of Allah's servants can be His son, whereas the Church, by deviating from the Gospel, fabricated this belief. The Islamic conception of life regarding the generous majesty of Allah is very lofty and exalted, and this "Kaniseh" is far above childish imaginings. The relationship of compassion and love between Allah and the servant is beyond human words. Along with the majesty of Allah it can be felt, but it cannot be described.

The overflowing of Allah's mercy reaches all His servants. This mercy embraces everyone in its shelter. It is through this mercy that the human self remains alive; the bond between his body and soul is firmly established. In the human existence and in the existence of this entire universe, the mercy of Allah and His generous majesty continually flow. As far as human life and the human body are concerned, we cannot count the occasions of Allah's mercy within them. Nevertheless, it is necessary to mention some of its outstanding aspects and manifestations.

First of all, the mercy of Allah is seen in the very self of man. Allah creates man in such a way that man himself has no knowledge of it. Human beings themselves do not know how this existence was granted to them. Then within him have been placed such distinctive qualities that through them man has been given superiority over all created beings.

Then His generous majesty is seen in the powers which man has, until today, been able to subdue. This universe and its powers, and this is Allah's provision in its broader meaning, may be understood thus: the universe, in whose vast fields man at all times displays his prowess.

Then the manifestation of this generous majesty is also seen in the fact that Allah bestowed knowledge upon man. First He granted him the capacity to acquire knowledge, and He created harmony between his faculties and the powers of this universe. This knowledge, by means of which some ill-natured and bad-tempered human beings begin to lay hands even upon the Divine Being, while it is He who conferred this knowledge upon those ill-natured people, and this knowledge is one of the provisions from Allah.

Then this generous majesty is also manifested in that Allah, by appointing man as His vicegerent in this world, arranged for his care and upbringing by sending messengers continuously for his guidance. Whenever man strayed, Allah guided him and, with great love and patience, set him again upon the straight path. Although at times man did not even give ear to the voices of those warning and admonishing messengers, it was not difficult for Allah to destroy him; yet the attribute of Allah's mercy always granted him respite, and always the forbearance of Allah covered man.

Then the manifestation of this generous majesty is also seen in the fact that when a servant commits a sin out of ignorance and then repents, Allah forgives him, and this is because Allah has made it binding upon Himself to show mercy.

It is also an aspect of His generous majesty that for an evil He records only one evil and punishes only for that one evil, but for a good deed He bestows the reward of ten good deeds, and beyond that He may increase for whomever He wills in his record of deeds. Moreover, Allah also keeps erasing the reward of good deeds, and all this is His bounty. Furthermore, no one can attain Paradise merely by the strength of his own deeds unless His grace is included in his favour. Even the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself said about himself that he too would enter Paradise by the grace of Allah. If the grace and bounty of Allah were not included, man would be most helpless.

In sum, rather than giving detailed accounts of the occasions and manifestations of Allah's mercy, generosity and bounty, it is better for us to declare our own shortcoming of understanding, and to say that it is difficult for us to fully comprehend His generous majesty, and that this is the appropriate attitude for us. For if we do not do so, and do not declare that we have failed, we cannot succeed in this field. The moment in which the doors of Allah's mercy open upon a servant, he attains access to Allah. He becomes filled with knowledge of his Lord; he attains peace and tranquillity. He takes refuge in the shelter of His compassion, and seeks refuge at His threshold. Even a single brief moment contains such vastness that it is not possible for any human being to describe or explain it; indeed, it is impossible for a person to fully express the generous majesty of Allah.

Consider carefully how the Noble Messenger (ﷺ), through his concise and comprehensive words and beautiful parables, sought to bring the generous majesty of Allah close to our understanding and our intellect. Al-Shaykhan, with their chains of narration, related from Abu Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu):

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: When Allah had decreed the creations (Imam Muslim said: when Allah had created the creatures), He wrote in a Book which is with Him upon the Throne: "My mercy has preceded My wrath." Imam al-Bukhari gave in another narration the words: "My mercy has overcome My anger."

Al-Shaykhan, through their chain, related from Abu Hurayrah (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah divided mercy into one hundred parts, of which He has retained ninety-nine with Himself, and has sent down upon the earth only one part. By using this one part, creatures show mercy to one another, so much so that an animal lifts its hooves lest it should step upon its young."

Imam Muslim, through his chain, related from Salman al-Farisi (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has one hundred mercies. By using one of these mercies, the creatures of Allah deal with one another with compassion, and Allah has reserved ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection."

In another narration from him: "On the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, He created one hundred mercies. Each mercy of Allah is greater than the heavens and the earth. Of these, Allah gave only one mercy for use upon the earth. By this mercy a mother shows compassion to her child, and wild animals and birds show mercy to one another. When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will complete this mercy with the remaining ninety-nine parts."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described the extent of mercy through images, only to bring it closer to human understanding. When a person observes among living creatures how mothers treat their children with such compassion, and how people show kindness to their children, and likewise to the elderly, the weak, the sick, relatives, friends and offspring, and also how birds and wild animals treat one another, he is overcome with amazement. Some of these scenes are so striking that they overwhelm a person, and he then reflects that this is only one part out of a hundred parts of Allah's generous mercy, and he becomes even more astonished. This method of explanation brings the matter close to people's minds. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ constantly made his Companions aware of this great mercy.

Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: Some female prisoners of war were brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Among them was a woman who was running about, and milk was flowing from her breasts. Whenever she found a child among the captive women's camp, she would seize it, press it to her stomach and nurse it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do you think this woman would throw her child into the fire?" We said: "By Allah, if she has the power not to do so (i.e., is not compelled), she would never do it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Know that Allah has more love for His servants than this woman has for her child." (Bukhari, Muslim)

How could it not be so? The compassion and tenderness this woman has for her child is a blessing of that mercy which Allah has bestowed upon the inhabitants of the earth from His vast mercy.

The teaching that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave his Companions of this kind resulted in his taking one step further and commanding his Companions to adopt the character of Allah in this matter. They were to treat one another with mercy and affection, show mercy to all living creatures of this world, and let a taste for love and compassion arise in their hearts, so that they would practise this taste in all their affairs, just as Allah deals with His creatures with mercy. This aspect of the teachings of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is extremely vibrant and radiant. Let us observe some examples.

Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that he said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Those who show mercy will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Show mercy to those on the earth, and He who is in the heavens will show mercy to you." (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi)

Narrated from Ibn Jarir (may Allah be pleased with him), who said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah does not show mercy to one who does not show mercy to people." (Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi)

Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi have stated, in a narration from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Mercy is taken away only from one who is hard-hearted."

Similarly, Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ kissed Hasan ibn Ali, and at that time Aqra ibn Habis was sitting beside him. Aqra said: "I have ten children, and I have never kissed any one of them." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked at him and said: "Whoever does not show compassion, compassion will not be shown to him." (Muslim, Bukhari)

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not merely teach his Companions to treat only human beings kindly, because he knew that Allah's mercy is very vast and that Muslims had been commanded to develop the character of Allah within themselves. A person cannot become a complete human being until he treats all creation with mercy. In this regard, his teachings were extremely effective, as we have already mentioned.

Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It happened that a man, during a journey, was walking along a path when he was overcome by severe thirst. He found a well, descended into it, drank water and came out. Then he saw a dog panting from thirst and eating earth because of the intensity of its thirst. The man said: 'This dog has been reduced to the same state by thirst as I had been.' So he went down into the well again, filled his shoe with water, held it in his mouth until he came out, and gave the dog water to drink. Allah accepted this from him, rewarded him and forgave him." The Companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there a reward for us in (showing kindness to) animals?" He ﷺ said: "There is a reward in (showing mercy to) every living creature with a moist liver." (Bukhari, Muslim, Muwatta)

In another narration, it is related that a sinful woman once saw a dog circling a well in intense heat, its tongue hanging out from thirst. She made a bucket of her shoe and a rope of her headscarf, drew water for it and gave it to drink, and Allah forgave her.

Abdul Rahman ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from his father, who said: We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a journey. We saw a bird (a humrah) with two young ones with it, and we seized the young ones. The bird came and was fluttering over the ground (that is, it was drawing close to the earth with its wings loosened and spread). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came and said: "Who has caused distress to her on account of her young? Return her young to her." He ﷺ also saw that we had burned an anthill, so he asked: "Who burned this?" We said: "We burned it." He ﷺ said: "No one should punish with fire except the Lord of the fire." (Abu Dawud)

Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A prophet was bitten by an ant. He ordered that its colony be burned. Allah revealed to him: 'Because an ant bit you, will you destroy an entire community which glorifies Allah?'" (Muslim, Bukhari)

In this way, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ trained his Companions, in accordance with this teaching of the Noble Qur'an, so that they would taste the mercy of Allah in such a way that they would extend it to people. Is it not a fact that the mercy and compassion which creatures show to one another is one of the countless and priceless mercies of Allah?

Now I wish to state that when the reality of mercy becomes settled in a Muslim's conception of life, it has profound effects on his feelings, his life and his character, and these can never be erased in any form. Here, in keeping with the concise style of Fi Zilal al-Quran, we shall also point out briefly the effects that the above teaching has on the life of a Muslim.

As a result of awareness of this reality, the heart of the believer is enriched with the wealth of tranquillity, and he becomes fully content with his Lord. This is especially so in circumstances when he is passing through difficulties and severe moments, because in trials and hardships a person's heart and sight may be deceived. Thus the believer, beset by difficulties, always hopes for the mercy of Allah and believes that circumstances can change at any moment, and that after every situation a new situation may arise. Allah does not abandon His servants to difficulties, nor deprive them of His mercy, because whoever seeks Allah's mercy, Allah will not deprive him. It is people who deprive themselves of Allah's mercy by being ungrateful to Him, refusing to come under the shade of His mercy, and fleeing from it. Then, through firm contentment in hope of Allah's mercy, patience and steadfastness arise within a person, the light of hope shines, and he feels ease and rest, because he is in the court of mercy and love whose shade is dense, so long as he does not himself distance himself from it.

When a Muslim attains this awareness, a sense of modesty before the Creator arises in his feelings, because despite hope for forgiveness and the desire for the mercy of the Lord, no one should dare to disobey Allah. Indeed, through this hope one should feel shame at disobeying Allah, the Forgiving and Merciful. Those in whom the mercy and forgiveness of Allah give rise to a further urge to commit sin have, in truth, never tasted the sweetness of the reality of faith. Therefore, neither do I understand, nor do I accept, what some Sufis say: that they commit sins so that they may taste Allah's forbearance and clemency, or benefit from His forgiveness and mercy. This is not the thinking of people of sound nature; it is a negative reaction to the mercy of God.

After grasping this reality in this manner, very good effects arise in the mind of a Muslim. He knows that he must develop within himself the character of Allah. He also knows that the showers of Allah's mercies are falling upon him from every direction, despite his being full of shortcomings and sins occurring from him. In this way, he himself learns the ways of mercy and tenderness; he knows how to forgive, he overlooks sins and mistakes. This is clearly visible to us in the teachings that the Messenger ﷺ gave to his Companions, and this teaching he imparted through "takhalluq bi-akhlaq Allah" (adopting the character of Allah). One of the stations of Allah's mercy is that He has written upon Himself that He will gather all human beings on a day in the field of assembly. This verse also decides this:

﴿Say: "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?" Say: "To Allah. He has prescribed mercy upon Himself. He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt."﴾ (6:12)

Included in this claim of Allah's written mercy is that He will gather them again on a day, and this is an unalterable reality. After this gathering, the favours of Allah will be manifest, and these favours will be for those who worship Him, because Allah created them precisely so that they would take the path of worshipping Allah throughout their whole lives. They were given the office of vicegerency on this earth solely for this purpose. They were not created without purpose, nor are they left aimless. There is a day coming on which all these people will be assembled. This is the final destination to which they will return, just as a caravan moves steadily toward its intended goal. There Allah will reward those who adopted the correct path toward Allah and bore hardships during this long journey of life. The good deeds they performed in the world will be recompensed there, so that their exertions and hardships are not lost, but rather they will be given their full reward on the Day of Judgment. Thus one of the manifestations of Allah's mercies will be displayed. The grace of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, whereby the recompense for an evil deed will be only its like, while the reward for a good deed will be ten times, and indeed, if Allah wills, multiplied many times over, will also be one of the manifestations of Allah's mercy and compassion.

The grace and generosity that Allah bestowed upon the Arabs through the religion of Islam, and the honourable station He gave them through this religion, is a great favour of Allah upon them. Before this, the Arabs denied the Resurrection. They held exactly the same ideas as the thinking of the modern civilised ignorance, that is, scientific ignorance. For this reason, the mention of the Resurrection was made in such emphatic words, and against this denial, such emphatic particles were brought.

﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt.﴾ (6:12)

On the Day of Resurrection, loss will befall only those who in this world remained deprived of faith. Those who believe will suffer no loss, whereas the disbelievers will suffer complete loss, because they have lost their very selves, so what will they earn? A person earns for his own soul and self. If his self and his tongue are gone, for whom will he earn, and for whom will he work?

﴿Those who have lost themselves, so they do not believe.﴾ (6:12)

"But those who have put themselves into the danger of ruin do not believe in it." They lost their very selves in loss; their self and personality went away, and since they no longer had any personality, who would believe? This is a very subtle and realistic expression of the condition of the disbelievers. Within this expression there is a deeply natural call: believe! One of the great blessings of faith is that it grants you a self and a personality. Those who lost their personality before faith, whose nature had been corrupted, whose capacities that accept truth had been destroyed or veiled, lost their identity and individuality by losing the capacity to accept truth. This is why they did not believe, because they no longer had their own self and personality. This is a very subtle and profound description of their lack of tranquillity and of their disbelief. Yet the proofs of faith were present, and there were indications by which a person accepts truth; this matter became decisive in their case. Thus, having washed their hands of their own personality, they suffered a barren loss.

Now the next verse tells us that the people and creatures of night and day, that is, of time, also belong to Him. Just as the earlier verses stated that whatever living being is in any place and any space is the possession of Allah, so ownership now encompasses both time and space. Allah's knowledge encompasses all creatures.

(وَلَهُ مَا سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ ۚ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ) "To Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." (6:13)

"Whatever dwells in the night and the day, all of it belongs to Allah, and He hears and knows everything." 

The most readily understood interpretation of (مَا سَكَنَ) is that it derives from sakana (to dwell, to take refuge), as Zamakhshari wrote in al-Kashshaf: that is, everything that takes refuge in night and day, meaning all creation. All of this creation is in Allah's ownership. The previous verse also established this: (قُل لِّمَن مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۗ قُل لِّلَّهِ) "Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To Allah." (6:12). That verse expressed the scope of all creation in terms of place, whereas this verse, (وَلَهُ مَا سَكَنَ فِي اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ) (6:13), expresses it in terms of time. This is a well-known mode of expression in the Holy Qur'an. Much has been written in the commentary of these verses, but in my view the best explanation is that one verse restricts ownership by time and the other by place.

After this comes the remark that Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, from which it is understood that, in respect of knowledge too, Allah encompasses all creatures. In response to this verse, whatever the polytheists say is within Allah's knowledge. That is, even while acknowledging that Allah alone is the Owner, they nevertheless set aside certain livestock, their young, and certain fruits for their partners. This discussion recurs at the end of this surah. Here Allah demands that people acknowledge His rightful ownership of all creation, so that later it may be explained to them by whose authority they assign some of Allah's creatures to the account of their partners. Along with this, the phrase also aims to establish that since He is the Owner, He is also the Guardian and the Ruler, and He is the Ruler because He is the Owner of everything within time and space, and within Allah's knowledge.

Now that it is established that He is the Creator and the Owner, severe rebuke and criticism is directed at those who seek help from anyone other than Allah, who worship anyone other than Allah, and who take others as guardians and rulers. Thus it is decided that this state of affairs is contrary to Islam; it is clear polytheism, and it cannot be combined with Islam. Here, to convey this meaning, attributes of Allah such as Fatir al-Samawat wal-Ard (Originator of the heavens and the earth), Razzaq and Mut'im (Provider and Feeder), Nafi' and Darr (the Benefiter and the Harmer), and Qahir and Qadir (the Subduer and the Powerful) are brought forth, while it is also stated that He inflicts a dreadful punishment. Thereupon the atmosphere is suddenly overshadowed by the majesty of Allah, the person is struck with fear, and this is said with great force:

This verse establishes that Allah alone is the walī (protector, guardian, helper) in every sense of the word. That is, He alone is the Lord, He alone is the object of worship, all people serve Him and all are subject to His sovereign authority. They worship Him and perform the rites of worship before Him. They regard Him alone as their helper and supporter, they place their trust in Him alone, and in calamities they turn to Him alone. This is the foundational belief of Islam. If a person regards Allah alone as his walī with all these meanings, then he is a Muslim; but if he makes someone else a walī alongside Allah, then he is a mushrik. Shirk and the walāyah (guardianship) of Allah alone cannot be combined in one heart.

This reality is expressed in this verse with great depth and profundity. Reflect on it once more.

(Verse) "Qul a-ghayra Allāhi attakhidhu waliyyan fāṭiri as-samāwāti wal-arḍi wa huwa yuṭʿimu wa lā yuṭʿamu. Qul innī umirtu an akūna awwala man aslama wa lā takūnanna mina al-mushrikīn." (14)

"Say: Shall I take as a walī other than Allah, the Creator of the heavens and the earth, who feeds and is not fed? Say: I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit, and you must not be among the mushrikīn."

This is a most profound, natural and logical line of thought. Who shall be a walī, and for whom shall guardianship be exclusive? If we do not take as our walī the One who created the heavens and the earth and brought them into existence, then whom shall we take? If the One who provides sustenance to all creatures living in the heavens and the earth is not our walī, then who else would be? He is the One who provides sustenance to all creation and needs no one himself.

Say: Shall I take other than Allah as walī, when Allah's being possesses the attributes that have been mentioned? The question is what argument and logic would compel a person to take someone other than Allah as walī. A person takes someone as walī and guardian because he helps him. Since Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and holds authority over both, if the purpose of guardianship and protection is that the protector provides sustenance and food, then the Being of Allah is the Provider and Feeder of all the worlds, whether they are on the earth or in the heavens. Now, what benefit would there be in taking someone other than Allah as walī and guardian?

Furthermore: "Say: I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit to Him, and I have been enjoined: you must not be among the mushrikīn." It becomes clear that submitting and abstaining from shirk necessarily mean not taking anyone other than Allah as guardian. From another angle, this conclusion follows: taking anyone other than Allah as guardian means that we are, as it were, committing shirk, and shirk can by no means be Islam.

This is a clear and definite matter. No ambivalence or leniency is possible regarding it. In this matter we can adopt only two positions. Either we regard Allah as one without partner, turn only toward Him, obey only Him, fear only Him, worship Him only with humility and submission, seek help only from Him, and regard Him alone as our sovereign, authority and lawgiver; obey Him in all the affairs of our life, associate no one with Him, and regard Him alone as our walī and guardian in our hearts and deeds, in our laws and conduct, not associating anyone with Him: then our attitude is pure Islam. Or else, if we associate any of His servants with Him in these matters, that attitude is mushrikīn, and shirk is a sickness and reality that cannot be combined with Islam in one place.

Allah ordered the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to openly declare his disapproval before the mushrikīn, because they were pressing him to show softness and compromise with them on this doctrinal issue, and to give their gods some standing within his religion. In exchange, they would enter this religion. Specifically, he would grant their gods some of the attributes of divinity, so that the status, rank and interests of the mushrikīn would remain intact. Above all and first of all, they wanted the right to make lawful and unlawful be given to their gods, and in return they would cease opposing the Messenger ﷺ, would accept him as the chief of Makkah, would pay him financial dues, and would give him their most beautiful daughters in marriage.

The mushrikīn of Makkah, on the one hand, tormented the Messenger ﷺ and inflicted cruelty upon the Muslims, and on the other hand, extended a hand of softness and reconciliation, seeking to entice him. Because of this policy of theirs, Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to declare before them his utmost abhorrence of these matters, and to announce decisively and in plain words that he could make no compromise in this doctrinal matter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 6, verses 15–16:

"Say: 'Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous Day.' Whoever is spared it on that Day, Allah has surely shown him mercy, and that is the manifest triumph." (6:15–16)

The Urdu text of the commentary reads as follows:

"If I disobey my Lord, I fear that I will suffer the punishment of a great day. On that day, whoever is spared from the punishment, Allah has shown him great mercy, and this is the clear success."

You are commanded to announce the importance and seriousness of this matter, and to say that if they deviate even a hair's breadth, the punishment of Allah may descend upon them too. Especially in matters of Islam and tawhid, this will create fear and awe in the hearts of the polytheists themselves.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was extremely sensitive regarding the commands of Allah, and this is the best depiction of it. It appears that the Messenger (ﷺ) feared the punishment of Allah greatly. Allah's punishment is so terrifying that if one is spared from it, merely being spared is considered a great triumph. Apart from this vivid sense, there is also in it a warning that shakes the hearts of the polytheists: both for the polytheists of that age and for the polytheists of later ages. This shows how dreadful the punishment of the Hereafter will be. This punishment will easily find its victim, will surround him, and will seize him in a swoop, and only the Almighty can save him. Since the reins of the punishment of Allah are in the hand of Allah, only He can turn it away. When a person reflects on this depiction, his breath begins to stop. How terrifying is that final moment. (For details, see my book *At-Tasweer al-Fanni fil-Quran*, the chapter "Tariqat al-Quran.")

The question is: why would anyone take someone other than Allah as a protector? Why would he entangle himself in this shirk and, as a result, entangle himself in such a dreadful punishment? Would he do so to gain some benefit for himself, or to save himself from some worldly harm, or so that people would help him in difficulties or give him some benefit in hardship? Yet benefit and harm are entirely in the hand of Allah. In the world of causes, it is Allah alone who possesses true power. All humans are under His power and control. In giving and withholding, only His wise plan is at work.
